searches.note: Twenty eight searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's. Twelve were restricted to a primary body's own domain and are read as primary through their summaries: daumas-gassac.com five times, masamiel.com and masamiel.fr four times, domainegauby.fr once, inao.gouv.fr with legifrance.gouv.fr once, and the Terrasses du Larzac and AOC Languedoc bodies with INAO once; one blocked the estate's own domains to find the ten year old elsewhere. Two searches on the making of Grange des Pères found nothing. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept in a record marked checked.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification and its year, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the bodies' own pages (the estates, INAO and Légifrance, the appellation bodies) for their own dates, rules and methods, then to the open web for the second source of each person's dates and each story beat.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source (the Gault Millau line not of the 1982 vintage, the 2004 recognition not on labels, the white of Grange des Pères, Muntada's vine ages, the ten year old's blend, years and serving); where a detail rested on no source found, it was cut or said with less (the Médoc manner, punching down, clay, other crops, the banker, the bush vines).
Sources whose title or address names a living person, or that are a writer's own site, were read in the results but never cited in the fragment or here.

tested: The first vintage, 1978, bottled in 1980 as Vin de Table, about four fifths Cabernet Sauvignon with Malbec, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Pinot and Tannat: the estate's 1978 sheet and its history page: confirmed.
Aimé Guibert (1924 to 2016), born in Millau: The Drinks Business gives Millau and 1924, a second notice gives 1924 to May 2016, Decanter and BKWine give his death in May 2016 at 91: confirmed.

The purchase at the start of the 1970s: Gault&Millau and Wine Spectator give 1970, the estate's timeline 1972 for the couple's choice of the valley; the start of the 1970s holds and founded stays empty.

Henri Enjalbert (1910 to 1983), a friend of the family and a Bordeaux geographer who urged the planting: an encyclopedic entry gives 20 January 1910 to 19 June 1983 and the HAL biobibliography the same; the estate calls him an Aveyronnais friend and professor at Bordeaux III: confirmed.
Émile Peynaud (1912 to 2004) advising the first vintage at a distance: the estate's history page: confirmed.

Gault Millau's Château Lafite of the Languedoc: the estate's history page gives October 1982, an estate PDF gives 1985; neither speaks of the 1982 vintage, which could not have been judged in October 1982: changed.
The white first made with the 1986 vintage: the estate's 1986 sheet and history page: confirmed; that vintage was Viognier, Muscat and Chardonnay, so the later varieties are said as later: changed.

Moulin de Gassac begun in 1991: the estate's history page (the Guilhem and Figaro labels of 1991): confirmed. Cuvée Émile Peynaud: created in 2001 and all Cabernet Sauvignon in the 2015 sheet: changed from led by.

The making: hand picking (the estate's harvest page), destemmed grapes and a long maceration of about three weeks with several pumpings over (the winery page), slow extraction, delicate pump over, twelve to fifteen months in barrels one to seven years old and no filtration (the 2022, 2023 and 2024 sheets): confirmed, and the Médoc manner, found in no source, cut.

Mondavi's withdrawal of May 2001 after two years of dispute, the Arboussas massif, Guibert's part in the defence association and a new municipality against the project: Decanter and the estate's hosted Midi Libre piece: confirmed.
The soil of glacial origin is the estate's own account after Enjalbert, which the plan asks to be told as such: the sites field now says so.

Serve, glass, label terms and ageing: the Codex's service reference for a full red; the estate's vintage notes give a youth of three to seven years, which fits opens after about seven: sound. The questions: one key each, options of one kind, explanations that teach: sound. Nobody living named; the sons and the widow are not named.

changed.was: At the start of the 1970s Aimé Guibert (1924 to 2016), born in Millau, and his wife bought the Daumas family's farm in the valley of the Gassac above Aniane. A friend, the Bordeaux geographer Henri Enjalbert (1910 to 1983), studied its red, powder fine soil of glacial origin and urged them to plant vines. They planted Cabernet Sauvignon, by the estate's account from cuttings of Bordeaux estates, and made their first vintage in 1978 with advice from the oenologist Émile Peynaud (1912 to 2004). It was bottled in 1980 as plain Vin de Table, mostly Cabernet with Malbec, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir and Tannat, since no appellation of the Languedoc allowed such a blend. As the estate tells it, Gault Millau called the 1982 the Lafite of the Languedoc, and a white followed with the 1986 vintage. In May 2001 the Californian house Mondavi gave up a plan to clear and plant the wooded Arboussas massif, common land of Aniane, after two years of dispute in which Guibert led the opposition and a new town council turned against the project. He died in 2016 and his sons carried the estate on. For a sommelier the wine is the founding case for fine Languedoc made outside the appellations.

changed.was: Before he planted a vine of his own, the founder of Grange des Pères worked in three cellars of note: with the Chave family in Hermitage, at Coche-Dury in Meursault and at Domaine de Trévallon in Provence. He then cleared stony limestone hills near Aniane and planted them from the late 1980s, taking his Syrah cuttings from Hermitage and his Cabernet Sauvignon from Trévallon, as most accounts tell it. The first vintage came in 1992, a red of Mourvèdre, Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon; Counoise appears in the later blends. Because Cabernet Sauvignon has no place in the Languedoc appellation, the wine was sold as a Vin de Pays de l'Hérault, the category since renamed IGP, as Mas de Daumas Gassac, a short way off, had been sold outside the appellations since 1978. The making held to one pattern: each variety picked and fermented apart, a long time in barrel, then a rest in vat, with no fining or filtering. A white of Roussanne, Marsanne and Chardonnay was made beside the red. The founder died in 2021, and his brother carried the domaine on. For a sommelier Grange des Pères and Daumas Gassac stand together as the Aniane pair: two estates that made their names in the Languedoc with no appellation behind them.

changed.was: Jonquières lies in the hills below the Larzac plateau in the Hérault, country whose growers long sent their grapes to the co-operative. In 1985 the founder, the son of a grower family, chose not to follow that road and set up his own estate in the village, bottling wine from its hill parcels under the Coteaux du Languedoc appellation. His father later made and bottled his own wine too, at Mas Cal Demoura in the same village. The house came to be counted among the pioneers of the Languedoc's revival, beside Mas de Daumas Gassac. The hills around it gained a name of their own: in 2004 Terrasses du Larzac first appeared on labels as a named part of the Coteaux du Languedoc, and a decree of 17 October 2014 made it an appellation in its own right, for red wine only. Autour de Jonquières, the house's principal red, takes its name from its making: a blend of about a dozen lieux-dits around the village and its neighbours. Before 2017 the blend also held Grenache and Cinsault; since then the founder has given more room to Mourvèdre beside Carignan and Syrah. For a sommelier it shows the Terrasses du Larzac as the hills make it: fresh, savoury and built to keep.

changed.was: Calce is a small village of the Agly valley, in the hills north west of Perpignan, where the Roussillon's dry reds long stood in the shadow of its vins doux naturels. A decree of 28 March 1977 created the Côtes du Roussillon Villages appellation, for red wine only, and gave the hill villages a name for their dry reds. In 1985, as most accounts date it, the founder took over his family's small holding of vines at Calce and began to make and bottle wine of his own. He farmed by organic principles and later by biodynamic ones, and the house came to leave much of its land wild, garrigue and woods with other crops among the vines. Over the years the house turned from power towards freshness, with whole bunches, little sulphur and less alcohol, and the estate was counted among the pioneers of dry Roussillon. Muntada, drawn from Grenache and Carignan of great age, became its flagship red, sold as Côtes du Roussillon Villages and raised for about thirty months in foudres and barrels. For a sommelier Muntada answers the guest who knows the Roussillon only for Banyuls and Maury: a dry red of the hills, fresh, supple and long.

The 10 Ans d'Âge: the estate's own range lists 20, 30 and 40 Ans d'Âge and single vintages and no 10 Ans d'Âge; merchants' sheets (Vin Coeur Catalan, Cave Ruthène) give the Cuvée Spéciale 10 Ans d'Âge as Grenache Noir 90, Macabeu 5 and Carignan 5 per cent, a year in glass bonbonnes outdoors and nine years in oak foudres, to serve at 14 to 16 degrees with blue cheese or chocolate desserts, keeping nearly twenty years: the record now teaches the ten year old by these and the swap is accepted.

The 20 Ans d'Âge: the estate's page gives Grenache Noir 90, Macabeu 5 and Carignan 5 per cent, a year in bonbonnes outdoors then at least twenty years in 350 hectolitre oak foudres, to serve at 15 degrees, opened an hour ahead: confirmed, and the patch for the swap rests on it.

Vintage Charles Dupuy: the estate's page gives Grenache of the Cabirou parcel planted in 1914, muted on the grains midway through fermentation and eighteen months in new barrels, in tribute to Charles Dupuy: confirmed; the banker cut.
Mutage traced by the house to a Montpellier physician of 1285: told as the house's, a hedge that stands.

The questions: a new distractor (bought at auction after the Revolution) in place of the family of bankers, which taught an unsourced word, and the explanation now says why the bridge is wrong: changed. The traps: Maury Sec, rancio and Banyuls against Maury: sound.

changed.was: As the house tells it, the estate began with a game of cards. In 1816 a Bishop of Perpignan staked the Domaine des Goudous at the table and lost it to an engineer of the state's roads and bridges service, whose surname, Amiel, the estate has carried since; nobody knows quite what passed at the table. Its wine rested on a far older idea, mutage, the stopping of fermentation with spirit, which the house traces to a Montpellier physician of 1285. Early in the twentieth century a banker bought the estate, and his family held it through the century until the last of the line died in 1997. The house made its name with Maury aged in the open air: Grenache muted with spirit, set out for a year in glass bonbonnes in sun and frost, then kept for years in the large old oak foudres of its cellar. In 1999 the estate was sold to a buyer from outside the family. Its range sets the oxidative wines beside a young, fruit led Vintage and dry reds. For a sommelier the ten year old shows the oxidative style of Maury plainly: Grenache turned towards prune, coffee and walnut by air and time.

Early in the twentieth century the Dupuy family took the estate over and held it through the century, until the last of the line died in 1997. The 20 Ans d'Âge has the estate's own page for its blend, its years in bonbonne and foudre and its serving, so every fact of the swapped record is primary.
